titre: Schiaparelli Spoke of Natural Channels, Lowell of Martian Engineers
accroche: In 1893, Schiaparelli writes that there is no need to see intelligent beings behind the canals of Mars. Lowell reads the same regularity the other way around.
contenu_vulgarise:
On September 5, 1877, Mars is at opposition near its perihelion, which brings it closer to Earth. In Milan, Giovanni Schiaparelli observes it with a 22-centimeter refractor and draws from it the first detailed map of the planet. It shows dark lines that he calls canali.

The word, people say, did it all: in Italian, canale can mean “canal,” “channel” or “conduit.” Translated as “canals,” it would have suggested dug works, and therefore builders. The explanation is widespread. It is not false, but it shifts the question, as Schiaparelli's text allows us to see.

## What Schiaparelli writes in 1893

In “Il pianeta Marte,” published in February 1893 in the journal Natura ed Arte, he describes these lines as the famous canals of Mars. He notes that their length and location do not vary, that their appearance changes from one opposition to the next, sometimes from one week to the next, and that none stops in the middle of a continent: each one opens onto a sea, a lake or another canal. He remarks that they darken and widen when the northern snows melt, at the oppositions of 1882, 1884 and 1886. He concludes that they are canals in fact and not just in name, a true hydrographic system.

Then he adds that there is no need to suppose in them the work of intelligent beings. Despite the almost geometric appearance of the whole, he leans for now toward seeing in them a product of the planet's evolution, like the English Channel and the Mozambique Channel on Earth.

## The same regularity, read backward

In 1895, the American Percival Lowell publishes Mars. A section of the chapter “Canals,” titled “Artificiality,” is devoted to the lines. Lowell argues there that the appearance of the lines is enough to rule out all the purely natural explanations put forward so far, on three counts: their straightness, their uniform width, their systematic radiation from particular points. Too great a regularity, he writes in essence, is in itself what most suggests that an intelligence is at work.

Schiaparelli had the same thing before his eyes. In the same article, speaking of the doubled canals, which he calls “geminations,” he writes that he will take care not to combat the idea of intelligent beings, which is not at all impossible. But he adds that the geometric appearance does not require it: nature itself produces geometry, in crystals, in Saturn's ring, in the rainbow. What separates the two men is therefore not just a badly translated word. It is what one does with an observed regularity.

## What Mars really showed

On July 14, 1965, the Mariner 4 probe takes 21 images of Mars, the first close-up views of another planet. NASA sums them up this way: an arid, crater-pocked planet, which dispelled the idea of intelligent life. Historians of science now see in the canals of the time an artifact of perception and language, tied to the limits of the telescopes and to optical illusions, with the possible exception of Valles Marineris, a real natural canyon.

What remains is a question the probes do not settle: why did experienced observers draw straight lines that the probes did not find?

repere.texte: In February 1893, Schiaparelli writes that there is no need to suppose here the work of intelligent beings, and that he leans toward a product of the planet's evolution. In 1895, Lowell devotes a section of his book Mars to the “Artificiality” of the lines, whose regularity would, in his view, rule out all purely natural causes.
repere.source: Schiaparelli, Il pianeta Marte, Natura ed Arte, 1893; Lowell, Mars, 1895, Chapter IV, section 3

carte.punch: The canals of Mars: Schiaparelli speaks of nature, Lowell of engineers.
carte.idee: In 1893, Schiaparelli describes the canals of Mars as real channels, and writes that there is no need to suppose intelligent beings behind them. In 1895, Lowell reads the same regularity as proof of the work of engineers.

pour_aller_plus_loin.note: In Italian; the complete article, with the description of the seas, lakes and canals.
In English; the “Artificiality” section begins on page 148.

quiz.question: What does Schiaparelli conclude in 1893 about the origin of the canals of Mars?
choix: They are real channels, probably born of the planet's evolution
They are works dug by intelligent beings to irrigate the planet
They are optical illusions caused by the limits of his telescope
They are ice cracks visible only when the snows melt
quiz.explication: Schiaparelli holds the canals to be real channels, and he writes that there is no need to suppose intelligent beings in them. The idea of dug works is Lowell's in 1895; that of optical illusions is the reading of today's historians; ice cracks do not appear in his text.

quiz_supplementaire.question: On what three counts does Lowell judge, in 1895, that the appearance of the Martian lines rules out any natural cause?
choix: Their straightness, their uniform width and their radiation from particular points
Their color, their length and their variation from one opposition to the next
Their doubling, their thickness and their disappearance in winter
Their alignment with the poles, their curvature and their symmetry
quiz_supplementaire.explication: In the Artificiality section of his book Mars (1895), Lowell singles out three counts, straightness, uniform width and radiation from particular points, and judges that such regularity betrays an intelligence.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What did the Mariner 4 probe show in 1965, according to NASA?
choix: An arid, crater-pocked planet, which dispelled the idea of intelligent life
Traces of liquid water in the canals observed by Schiaparelli
An atmosphere too dense to make out the ground
quiz_supplementaire.explication: On July 14, 1965, Mariner 4 takes 21 images, the first close-up views of another planet, and NASA sums up the result as an arid, crater-pocked planet, which dispels the idea of intelligent life.
